360	And I said that the Rebbe's bowl was made of cloth — I mean before
361	the Rebbe accepted the leadership, in the Rebbe Rayatz's lifetime.
362	As a Rebbe he had a silver bowl, but
363	for our purposes,
364	the poor
365	would bring what they could afford, in straw baskets. They would
366	of course choose a nice basket,
367	well made, maybe even — I assume, it's quite
368	simple for me to think so — that everyone would find in himself
369	the delight of preparing the basket himself, if he
370	only could, and making it
371	with extra care and precision.
372	But in the end, a straw basket.
373	>> Rabbi, there is a repair somewhere that...
374	>> Surely, everything I am saying now, I am not inventing it.
375	It is all, not in pictures.
376	>> Pictures — there were none. We are talking about the last time
377	the mitzvah of Bikurim was fulfilled, which was
378	about 1,960 years ago, in the time of the Second Temple.
379	>> And there were no photographs yet. There were drawings, but not
380	photographs, nor drawings since then, though drawings could
381	be made. Yes, so it could be drawn today. There are no drawings
382	preserved since then, to my knowledge at least. Also
383	then there was no paper, so there was nothing to draw on.
384	Now,
385	the novelty was that precisely with the poor,
386	the basket too would remain in the Beit HaMikdash.
387	They would not take it back home, but every year
388	they would bring to the Beit HaMikdash not only the fruits but also
389	the basket; the holiness would actually penetrate this basket too.
390	It was an advantage of the poor over the rich. With
391	the rich it looked much more beautiful.
392	The picture of the king bringing the Bikurim is not
393	in a straw basket, but in a basket of gold. But
394	with all due respect, he takes the basket back.
395	Whereas the poor, everything they brought to HaShem,
396	HaShem accepts all of it.
397	In any case,
398	every first fruit — or "a lot, good luck." The quantity was
399	an enormous quantity, or...
400	>> The quantity was not enormous, but it was indeed
401	every first fruit, roughly in the proportion of one percent,
402	or a bit more than one percent of all the fruits, but it
403	could be a significant basket in the end. Yes.
404	Surely there is even a halachic definition of the order of
405	the fruits, so that the fruits — for example the grapes must
406	be on top, because if they were below they would of course
407	be crushed. Only from the seven kinds.
408	>> Only from the seven kinds. Now,
409	whoever wanted to beautify his basket
410	even more would tie turtledoves and young pigeons to it.
411	Picture to yourselves how that looks: a basket with
412	turtledoves and young pigeons tied to it, like doves.
413	>> They were real doves, surely, which they bring
414	as an offering to HaShem...
415	>> Yes, they would do it in a way that would not harm them.
416	>> Now, anyway, what is the point? The point is
417	that merely mentioning this mitzvah
418	already fills us with a feeling of joy
419	and warmth, because it is truly an extraordinary mitzvah.
420	We have no example. What? The closest example
421	to this mitzvah today, in terms of the heartfelt emotion that accompanies
422	this mitzvah, and the preparation, and the training, and the connection,
423	the feeling of connection to HaShem, the closest we have,
424	this thing is really the experience of the Pesach Seder, with all
425	the preparations made for the Seder, with all the splendor
426	on the Seder table, with the Haggadah. And why do I say
427	the Haggadah? Because it is really the high point, it is what
428	we began to say before, the high point.
429	For a whole group comes, sometimes dozens or
430	perhaps hundreds of Jews, each one coming with his basket of
431	Bikurim, on the same day, in the same
432	procession,
433	and
434	each one places his basket. But it does not
435	end there; each one waits for his turn.
436	And when it arrives,
437	the turn of the girl, as it is written in the Megillat Esther, when it arrives
438	the turn of the specific person
439	who brought his basket of Bikurim,
440	then he reads the Mikra Bikurim, which is detailed
441	in the Parashah: "And you shall speak up and say before HaShem your Elokim."
442	And the Jew reads the Mikra Bikurim with emotion of
443	joy,
444	with tremendous excitement.
445	And who listens to him? Everyone. That is, at that moment
446	he is at the center of attention, and everyone, all the Kohanim
447	gather around him, everyone listens to him, all
448	the Jews who came together with him, everyone listens. One by one,
449	each one gets all the space, all the...
450	>> This reminds me of something, as a complete aside,
451	but something, an experience like this, where each one receives the
452	most exalted privilege.
453	>> With the Rebbe. What is there with the Rebbe in this matter?
454	Not that the Rebbe gives each one a dollar, or a lekach, or
455	a blessing. That gaze of the Rebbe on you for two
456	seconds is something very, very special, but
457	in the end it is something the Rebbe gives you. That the Rebbe gives
458	every Jew the feeling that he is a king, that he is the most important
459	and most precious thing to him — that is no novelty, because it is truly so
460	>> In those seconds.
461	>> In those seconds. But there is something closer to what
462	we are now describing, which is a once-in-a-lifetime privilege,
463	and it is the privilege of grooms.
464	Every groom, before the day of his wedding, has one
465	single opportunity in which the Rebbe gives him his personal siddur
466	to pray the Mincha prayer from it.
467	So think what excitement it is to stand
468	and receive the Rebbe's siddur.
469	In the times when we merited to see the Rebbe, it was receiving
470	the siddur from the Rebbe's holy hands. Not everyone
471	would receive it either, because if there were several
472	grooms, the Rebbe would ask who is older, or who is a Kohen,
473	or who... he would not give it, and they would pass it from one
474	to another. But in the end each one stands for the duration of
475	the Mincha prayer, which can be a significant time,
476	and prays from the Rebbe's siddur, and of course it is
477	the prayer in which you ask for everything you want to ask
478	for your whole life, not only for yourself but for the bride too.
